ai-at-work.title: Harvard’s $699 startup bootcamp offers AI avatars of its instructors
ai-at-work.excerpt: In the HBS Foundry program, AI avatars provide feedback during practice pitches and board meetings.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Harvard Business School is charging $699 for a startup bootcamp where AI avatars of actual instructors provide feedback on your pitch practice and mock board meetings. This matters because it shows how institutions are experimenting with AI-scaled expertise, which means digital workplace leaders need to start thinking seriously about where human judgment still creates real value versus where it's just expensive theatre. Honestly, if an AI avatar can tell you your pitch needs work, so can your coworker for free, but I respect HBS for at least being transparent about what you're actually getting instead of pretending the avatar is the real deal.

ai-at-work.title: Inherent, founded by DeepMind alumni, says its AI ‘teammate’ just outperformed Anthropic and OpenAI at replicating research
ai-at-work.excerpt: Built by DeepMind alumni, British AI lab Inherent released Faraday, an AI agent whose ability to replicate scientific papers could be a stepping stone for innovation.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Inherent, a UK startup founded by former DeepMind engineers, released an AI agent called Faraday that allegedly outperforms Claude and ChatGPT at reproducing scientific research findings. This matters because if AI can reliably replicate complex research work, it changes how knowledge workers validate findings and accelerate discovery across industries. That said, replicating papers in controlled lab conditions is very different from handling the messy, ambiguous work that actually pays salaries in most organizations, so let's pump the brakes on the revolution rhetoric until someone shows this works with your actual research backlog.

ai-at-work.title: Railway secures $100 million to challenge AWS with AI-native cloud infrastructure
ai-at-work.excerpt: Railway, a San Francisco-based cloud platform that has quietly amassed two million developers without spending a dollar on marketing, announced Thursday that it raised $100 million in a Series B fundi
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Railway just scored $100 million to build cloud infrastructure specifically designed for AI workloads, positioning itself as a leaner alternative to AWS for developers who are tired of enterprise bloat. This matters because digital workplace teams are increasingly wrestling with how to deploy AI applications efficiently, and having competitive infrastructure options means better pricing and tools built for modern use cases instead of retrofitted legacy systems. The fact that they grew to two million developers without spending on marketing tells you something important: when your product actually solves a real problem better than the incumbents, people show up.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic launches Cowork, a Claude Desktop agent that works in your files — no coding required
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic released Cowork on Monday, a new AI agent capability that extends the power of its wildly successful Claude Code tool to non-technical users — and according to company insiders, the team bui
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic just dropped Cowork, an AI agent for Claude Desktop that lets regular people automate file work without touching a line of code. This matters because we're finally seeing AI tools that don't require you to become a developer first, which means your entire workforce could theoretically handle their own workflow automation. The real question is whether people will actually use it or if it joins the graveyard of "powerful tools nobody knows how to integrate into their actual job."

tools-tech.title: Google's new Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags (and they cost the same)
tools-tech.excerpt: Google's new finder tags use an emerging Bluetooth technology to offer more precise tracking - and stand apart from Apple and Samsung in the process.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Google launched Pixel Tags that use newer Bluetooth tech to track items more precisely than AirTags, at the same price point. This matters because workplace IT teams suddenly have another choice for asset tracking and device location in hybrid environments, plus it chips away at Apple's ecosystem lock-in that many organizations grudgingly accept. Honestly though, in 30 years I've seen a lot of tracking solutions come and go, and the real question isn't the technology, it's whether your org actually commits to using these things consistently instead of letting them gather dust in a drawer.

digital-culture.title: AI has young writers between a rock and a hard place
digital-culture.excerpt: Buzzwords, clichéd phrases, formulaic sentences, and most notoriously—the use of the em dash. These are all signs readers and writers alike have learned to look out for when trying to spot whether som
digital-culture.dwp_take: Young writers are getting accused of using AI simply because their work contains common writing patterns that detection tools flag as suspicious. This matters because it's creating a trust crisis in digital workplaces where writing quality is getting confused with writing origin, and managers are second-guessing legitimate human work. Here's the kicker: the real problem isn't AI detection, it's that we've collectively decided formulaic writing equals AI, when honestly, a lot of human writers have always been formulaic.

digital-culture.title: When loving where you work becomes a problem
digital-culture.excerpt: Below, Claire Stapleton shares five key insights from her new book, Don’t Be Evil: Bad Bosses, Fake Promises, and My Escape From Big Tech. Stapleton spent 12 years at Google, joining straight out of c
digital-culture.dwp_take: Claire Stapleton's new book details her twelve-year journey at Google, from college hire to senior YouTube leader, culminating in her organizing the 2018 walkout over sexual harassment handling. This matters because it illustrates how even the most lovable employer brands can mask serious cultural dysfunction, a lesson every digital workplace leader needs to absorb. The irony is brutal: the company that mastered employee engagement and perks culture turned out to be pretty good at using them as a smokescreen.

industry-news.title: Vibe Coding Goes Mainstream: Meta Brings AI Creation to Social Media
industry-news.excerpt: Meta’s Pocket app turns AI-generated games and interactive experiences into social content users can play, remix, and share in a scrolling feed. The post Vibe Coding Goes Mainstream: Meta Brings AI Cr
industry-news.dwp_take: Meta launched Pocket, an app that lets users create AI-generated games and interactive experiences to share on social feeds, turning what used to require actual coding skills into a point-and-click operation. This matters because it signals that AI creation tools are moving from niche developer playgrounds into mainstream social consumption, which means your workplace communication strategies need to account for users who expect to consume and create rich interactive content at work. Honestly, we're about two years away from someone pitching a critical business process as an "immersive AI game experience" and everyone pretending that's not just a fancy way to avoid reading an email.

industry-news.title: Meta Smart Glasses Under Fire: UK Cinemas Consider New Restrictions
industry-news.excerpt: UK cinemas are considering restrictions on Meta smart glasses over piracy and privacy concerns, raising questions about accessibility and recording. The post Meta Smart Glasses Under Fire: UK Cinemas
industry-news.dwp_take: UK cinemas are considering banning Meta smart glasses due to piracy and privacy concerns, which would restrict people from wearing them in theaters. This matters to digital workplace professionals because it signals how fast regulatory friction can mount around new wearable tech, forcing organizations to think harder about device policies and acceptable use before they become mainstream. Here's the thing though: if we're going to ban glasses because someone might record a film, we'd better start frisking people for phones, and good luck with that conversation.

industry-news.title: ChatGPT Is Suddenly Citing Reddit Far Less: Here’s What Changed
industry-news.excerpt: ChatGPT citations to Reddit plunged in August as its search behavior shifted, raising new questions about how websites earn visibility in AI answers. The post ChatGPT Is Suddenly Citing Reddit Far Les
industry-news.dwp_take: OpenAI's ChatGPT dropped its reliance on Reddit as a source in August, apparently shifting its search and citation patterns without explanation. This matters because it shows how AI training and search algorithms can suddenly reshape which websites get traffic and visibility, meaning your content strategy needs to account for forces you can't always predict or control. After years of Reddit being treated like gospel by these systems, watching it get ghosted overnight is a good reminder that betting your workplace content entirely on any single platform is about as smart as building your house on sand.

industry-news.title: Slack Code: AI Coding Agents Get Shared Channels for Review and Oversight
industry-news.excerpt: Slack Code gives AI coding agents shared project channels where teams can watch, guide and review software development as it happens. The post Slack Code: AI Coding Agents Get Shared Channels for Revi
industry-news.dwp_take: Slack just rolled out Slack Code, which puts AI coding agents into shared channels so teams can actually see what the bot is building and jump in when needed. This matters because it addresses the real tension between moving fast with AI and not waking up one day to discover your codebase got rewritten by a robot with no guardrails. Finally someone's trying to make AI development transparent instead of just hoping for the best and calling it "innovation."
